**Why this matters:** NWM data are organized differently from SWOT and USGS data: by forecast run and forecast
hour, in files that cover the whole country. This reading explains that organization and gets your software ready,
so the session can go straight to retrieving forecasts. About 10 minutes, plus setup time. **Do the setup before the
session.**

## What you'll retrieve

The NOAA National Water Model (NWM) simulates and forecasts streamflow for about 2.8 million river reaches across the
United States. In Session 4 you retrieve NWM forecasts for the reach of the Ohio River at Louisville, Kentucky, both
today's forecast and archived forecasts issued during the April 2025 flood.

NWM output is stored as NetCDF files, one per forecast hour, each covering every reach in the model. The full model
output has no general-purpose query service in front of it: you read the files from NOAA's archive, mirrored on
Google Cloud and AWS. NOAA's experimental [NWM API](https://api.water.noaa.gov/nwm/v1/docs) serves individual reaches,
but only the most recent few days of forecasts.

The lesson focuses on NWM **forecasts** (short, medium and long range), because forecasting is what sets the NWM
apart: it predicts what rivers will do, everywhere, rather than recording what they did at a few places.

## Two terms you'll see in every route

- **Configuration:** which forecast product, e.g. `short_range` (hourly out to 18 hours, issued every hour),
  `medium_range` (out to 10 days, issued every 6 hours, with several *ensemble members*: parallel runs from slightly
  different inputs, numbered by `member_id`, that show the spread of possible outcomes), `long_range`, or
  `analysis_assim` (the model's best estimate of current conditions).
- **Reference time:** model initialization time, in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). NWM shorthand writes the
  reference hour with a Z for UTC: `00Z` is 00:00 UTC, and file names write it as `t00z`. The time each forecast value
  applies to is its **valid time** (`valid_datetime` in the API, `value_time` in `hydrotools`, `time` in the files).

All routes return the NWM's variable `streamflow`, in m³/s (the API labels it `CMS`), for each reach. The NWM has no
per-value data quality flag, so you record the configuration, reference time and model version with your data
instead.

## Reaches are identified by COMID

The NWM's location identifier is the **COMID** of a reach (also called `feature_id`, `nwm_feature_id` or ComID), a
number from the NHDPlus stream network. Before you can download a forecast, you find the COMID for your location. You
do this with the NLDI (Network Linked Data Index), a separate web service from wherever the NWM files live, called
from Python with the [`pynhd`](https://docs.hyriver.io/readme/pynhd.html) package (part of HyRiver).

## Setup: the lesson's environment

If you use the hosted HydroShare environment, pick the `Python (m03-nwm)` kernel and skip the commands below; on your own computer, `cd` into the unzipped learner bundle first (see "Two ways to run the course notebooks" in the Session 3 pre-reading).

The `m03-nwm` conda environment installs everything for discovery (`pynhd`) and for all three download routes
(`requests` for the NWM API, `hydrotools.nwm_client`, and `kerchunk` + `xarray` + `fsspec`), plus `matplotlib` for the
figures and `ipykernel` for Jupyter. The file is in the learner bundle as
`module-03_lesson-02_retrieve-noaa-nwm-data_environment.yml`.

```bash
conda env create -f module-03_lesson-02_retrieve-noaa-nwm-data_environment.yml
conda activate m03-nwm

# Optional: register this environment as a Jupyter kernel, then pick "Python (m03-nwm)" in Jupyter
python -m ipykernel install --user --name m03-nwm --display-name "Python (m03-nwm)"
```

If you work in Jupyter, choose the `Python (m03-nwm)` kernel; otherwise your notebook runs in a different environment
and imports such as `pynhd` fail. **None of the routes in this lesson needs an API key or account.**

The environment file pins the Python version but lets most packages float to their latest release, so a year from now
`conda env create` may give you newer versions than the ones we tested. When you finish an analysis, record exactly
what you ran with `conda env export > environment-lock.yml` and keep that file with your results. The examples were
tested with Python 3.14, `pynhd` 0.20.0, `hydrotools.nwm_client` 9.2.1, `kerchunk` 0.2.10, `xarray` 2026.9.0, `zarr`
3.4.0 and `fsspec` 2026.9.0.

## Key terms

- **NHDPlus:** the National Hydrography Dataset Plus, a geospatial dataset of the U.S. stream network, broken into
  reaches each with a COMID. The NWM runs on this network.
- **Catchment:** the land area that drains directly to one stream reach. Each NHDPlus reach has one catchment, which
  is why a point on the map can be looked up to find its COMID.
- **Lead time:** how far ahead a forecast value is: its valid time minus its reference time.
- **Long-format table:** a table with one row per value, where columns such as location, time or ensemble member say
  which value it is.
